Five developments in the filing are dated to a specific day or month in 2025.

**April 23, 2025: EU Digital Markets Act, Article 5(4) investigation (Item 3)**
The European Commission fined Apple €500 million and issued a cease-and-desist order requiring it to remove technical and commercial restrictions that prevent developers from steering users to distribution channels outside the App Store. Apple has appealed the decision.

**April 23, 2025: EU Digital Markets Act, Article 6(4) investigation (Item 3)**
The Commission issued preliminary findings in this separate investigation, which concerns Apple's new contractual requirements for third-party app developers and app marketplaces. A final finding of violation could lead to a cease-and-desist order and fines of up to 10% of Apple's annual worldwide net sales.

**April 30, 2025: Epic Games litigation (Item 3)**
The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California found Apple in violation of the 2021 injunction. The court barred Apple from charging any commission or fee on purchases consumers make outside an app and from restricting how developers guide users to those purchases. It also denied Apple's motion to narrow or vacate the injunction and referred the matter to the U.S. Attorney to determine whether criminal contempt proceedings are appropriate. Apple's request to stay the ruling pending appeal was denied, but the Ninth Circuit agreed to expedite the appeal.

**September 2, 2025: Google search licensing remedies (Risk Factors)**
This development involves Google, a commercial partner. Apple earns revenue from licensing arrangements under which Google and other companies offer their search services on Apple's platforms. After finding on August 5, 2024 that Google violated U.S. antitrust laws, the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia ordered certain remedies on September 2, 2025. The order remains subject to further proceedings and to appeal by the DOJ and Google. A reversal could impose remedies the DOJ originally proposed, such as barring Google from offering Apple commercial terms for search distribution, which could materially hurt Apple's ability to earn that revenue.

**October 2025: Ninth Circuit oral argument (Item 3)**
The Ninth Circuit heard oral arguments on Apple's expedited appeal of the Epic Games injunction ruling. The filing does not report a decision.

The filing dates some related items only to a quarter, so I excluded them: settlements of certain ordinary-course matters in Q4 2025, U.S. tariff actions beginning in Q2 2025, and the Section 232 semiconductor investigation, which has no stated date. Apple's fiscal 2023 10-K gives these causes, drawn from the "Business Seasonality and Product Introductions" discussion in Item 1 and the "Financial Risks" section of Item 1A:

1. **Seasonal holiday demand.** Net sales have historically been higher in the first fiscal quarter than in other quarters, due in part to holiday demand.
2. **New product and service introductions.** These can significantly affect net sales, cost of sales and operating expenses.
3. **Channel inventory cycles.** Indirect distribution channels are refilled with new inventory after a launch, and their stock of an older product often declines as a newer product's launch approaches.
4. **Anticipated introductions.** Net sales can be affected when consumers and distributors anticipate a product introduction.
5. **Dependence on a single product.** A significant portion of net sales comes from one product, so a decline in its demand could significantly affect quarterly net sales.
6. **Unexpected developments.** These include lower-than-anticipated demand for products or services, problems with new product or service introductions, IT system failures or network disruptions, and failure of a logistics, component supply or manufacturing partner.

The filing also notes that fiscal 2023 spanned 53 weeks, with the extra week in the first fiscal quarter. Apple adds an extra week every five or six years to realign its fiscal quarters with calendar quarters. The fiscal-period discussion does not say how much this affected net sales.

The filing ties the charges to a second-quarter 2020 reevaluation of goodwill and indefinite-lived intangibles, most significantly for PCC, in light of the severe initial effects of COVID-19 on commercial airlines and aircraft manufacturers. Before the reevaluation, PCC-related goodwill was carried at about $17 billion and PCC-related indefinite-lived intangibles at about $14 billion, substantially all recorded when Berkshire acquired PCC in 2016. The resulting pre-tax charges were $10.0 billion for goodwill and $638 million for indefinite-lived intangibles, about $10 billion of which related to PCC (Form 10-K, pages K-62 to K-63).

Berkshire says it considered several factors "including but not limited to": airline announcements about potential future demand, employment levels and aircraft orders; manufacturer announcements of reduced aircraft production; and actions Berkshire was taking or might take to restructure operations.

Under the prevailing circumstances, Berkshire deemed it "prudent" to increase discount rates and reduce prior long-term forecasts of future cash flows for impairment review purposes. The filing's policy explains why these inputs produced a charge: an impairment is recorded when carrying value exceeds fair value. For indefinite-lived intangibles, the full excess is charged to earnings. For a reporting unit, the excess is charged up to the carrying amount of goodwill. The filing also notes that fair value estimates for reporting units are significantly affected by assumptions about the severity, duration and long-term effects of the pandemic, and that such estimates can vary widely. The passage does not quantify the revised discount rates or forecast reductions.

Berkshire's 2022 10-K attributes PCC's 2021 revenue decline of $853 million (11.6%) to the COVID-19 pandemic. The MD&A says the pandemic contributed to material declines in commercial air travel and OEM aircraft production in both 2021 and 2020. It states that PCC's revenues were negatively affected in both years by reduced aircraft production levels, which reflected order delays and cancellations by airlines and inventory reduction initiatives within the industry (MD&A, Industrial products, p. K-49). The filing does not quantify how much each factor contributed.

More broadly, the business description says the pandemic had significant adverse effects on PCC's aerospace business in 2020 and 2021. Sudden and material reductions in air travel led to aircraft build-rate reductions and customer destocking at extraordinary rates. The filing also says that production delays in Boeing's 737 MAX and 787 programs during this period adversely affected PCC over the past three years (Item 1, Precision Castparts, p. K-12).

The earnings discussion also cites restructuring costs and production inefficiencies tied to the reduction in production. Even so, PCC's 2021 pre-tax earnings rose 78.8% to $1.2 billion. Boeing's 2024 Form 10-K links lower commercial airplane deliveries to four causes. BCA deliveries, including intercompany deliveries, were 348 in 2024 versus 528 in 2023 (p. 33).

The first is the IAM 751 work stoppage, which began September 13, 2024 and ended with a new contract ratified November 4, 2024. The filing says it "significantly reduced aircraft deliveries in the second half of 2024" (p. 24). The second is the ongoing safety and quality improvement actions Boeing is taking after the January 5, 2024 Alaska Airlines 737-9 accident. The third is supply chain constraints. The cash flow discussion lists the accident actions, supply chain constraints and the IAM 751 work stoppage together as reasons for lower deliveries (pp. 42, 44). The fourth is delays associated with business-class seats on the 787 program, which the filing says "adversely impacted 2024 deliveries" and will continue to affect in 2025 (p. 37).

I did not count causes the filing ties only to production rates, costs or revenue. These include the FAA's limit on 737 production rate increases beyond 38 per month, the slowed production rates on the 767 and 777X, reach-forward losses on the 777X and 767, and 737-9 customer considerations, which the filing ties to lower revenue and operating losses. I also excluded 777X delivery delays, since that program has not yet delivered any aircraft, and the 737-7 and 737-10 certification timing, which the filing links to financial results rather than deliveries. China trade tensions and possible government funding lapses appear only as future risks. Aircraft in inventory awaiting delivery in 2025 are not tied to the 2024 decline.
